# Pathogen Genes
Custom strains are built from recovered [bold]genes[/bold], not from any known civilian illness. Cellular substrate is only an inert binder for assembly; it does not make the finished organism Flu, wound sepsis, or any other catalogued station pathogen.
Synthesis can only tolerate so much genetic load at once. Some markers are mutually exclusive. While you assemble a recipe, the synthesizer projects a [bold]strain forecast[/bold]: transmission, clinical course, symptoms, organ targets, and treatment susceptibility.
Complexity ratings in parentheses indicate relative synthesis burden.
## Transmission
- [bold]Contact persistence[/bold] (1): favors infection through surface contact. - [bold]Airborne adaptation[/bold] (2): enables aerosol spread. Will not combine with sterilant resistance. - [bold]Enteric adaptation[/bold] (1): enables foodborne and ingestion routes. - [bold]Aerosol stability[/bold] (2): survives longer in air and needs less dose to take hold.
## Environmental
- [bold]Environmental growth[/bold] (1): lingers longer on surfaces and waste. - [bold]Environmental persistence[/bold] (2): strong resistance to natural decay; mild sterilant hardiness. - [bold]Sterilant resistance[/bold] (2): markedly blunts sterilants. Will not combine with airborne adaptation.
## Timing and virulence
- [bold]Culture yield[/bold] (1): shortens the silent incubation phase. - [bold]Slow incubation[/bold] (1): lengthens incubation and slightly softens infectivity. Will not combine with heightened virulence. - [bold]Heightened virulence[/bold] (2): raises lethality and infectivity. Will not combine with slow incubation.
## Symptoms and shedding
- [bold]Cough shedding[/bold] (1): cough-driven spread. Will not combine with sneeze shedding. - [bold]Sneeze shedding[/bold] (1): sneeze-driven spread. Will not combine with cough shedding. - [bold]Respiratory distress[/bold] (2): shortness of breath and asphyxiation stress. Will not combine with hemorrhagic expression. - [bold]Hemorrhagic expression[/bold] (2): bleeding and toxin stress. Will not combine with respiratory distress.
## Organ tropism
Only one organ tropism can be expressed in a single strain:
- [bold]Hepatic tropism[/bold] (1): favors liver tissue. - [bold]Pulmonary tropism[/bold] (2): favors lung tissue and worsens breathing. - [bold]Cardiac tropism[/bold] (2): favors heart tissue and adds toxin stress.
## Treatment vulnerability
A custom strain has [bold]no documented drug regimen[/bold] unless vulnerability markers are included. Omitting them makes clearance harder for Medical, but also denies you an easy read of a cure path from your own forecast.
- [bold]Antiviral vulnerability[/bold] (1): susceptible to Sol antiviral. Will not combine with ribavirin vulnerability. - [bold]Ribavirin vulnerability[/bold] (2): susceptible to ribavirin. Will not combine with antiviral vulnerability. - [bold]Ceftriaxone vulnerability[/bold] (1): susceptible to ceftriaxone. Will not combine with amoxla vulnerability. - [bold]Amoxla vulnerability[/bold] (1): susceptible to amoxla. Will not combine with ceftriaxone vulnerability.
Reservoirs bias what you find. Vent airways favor airborne and antiviral markers. Waste favors enteric routes and antibiotics. Blood and medical residue favor virulence and treatment-vulnerability isolates.
